For example, Sahakyan et al. (2008) (Experiment 3) found that although memory following an R-cue was enhanced by spacing (vs. massing) of half the items in each list, this also brought about greater List 1 costs after the F-cue.
In relation to directed forgetting, it has been reported that subjects employ a range of strategies to forget the first list (Gamboa et al., 2017; Sahakyan et al., 2008).
Sahakyan et al. (2008) explained their findings by reference to the idea that spacing (vs. massing) leads to the storage of additional context information.

Via a series of psychological [25, 26] and neural recording [11] experiments, researchers have shown that asking a subject to forget a list of items leads to worse memory by means of a rapid change of internally generated context.
Some support for the context-based account in free recall can be found in a study by Sahakyan, Delaney, and Waldum (2008).
If context is instrumental in either remembering or forgetting items on an immediate free recall test (Sahakyan et al., 2008), how does its role change when the same items are tested at a delay?

It may be worthwhile in future work to use well-learned twice-presented items to see if number of presentations is a crucial moderator variable, especially given that Sahakyan et al. (2008) used twice-presented items in their failure to obtain a spacing effect after directed forgetting.

The prediction of a smaller spacing effect at a delay was based in part on the study by Sahakyan et al. (2008), which suggests that a change in context occurs when items are tested at a delay, implying that the context-bound spaced items should be more poorly recalled at a delay.

Their conclusion was based in part on the SAM-based account of the list-strength effect proposed by Malmberg and Shiffrin (2005), and in part on the findings from Sahakyan et al. (2008), who showed that directed forgetting was larger for spaced items than massed items in a free recall paradigm.
While intentional forgetting produced faster forgetting of spaced than massed items (see Sahakyan et al., 2008), the passage of time seemed to produce parallel forgetting of spaced and massed items.
If participants encoded more context features in the list-oriented group, then also the effects of changing context should be more dramatic in this condition (e.g., Sahakyan et al., 2008).

Particularly, Sahakyan, Delaney, and Waldum (2008) showed that depth of encoding manipulations produce equivalent directed forgetting across more elaborately encoded and less elaborately encoded items, despite producing overall differences in recall.

Indeed, in prior research, Sahakyan et al. (2008) demonstrated that items that contain greater amounts of context in their memory trace (such as spaced items, Malmberg & Shiffrin, 2005), produce greater directed forgetting.

Rehearsal borrowing is a serious problem for list-strength studies, and solutions like using incidental learning (e.g., Sahakyan et al., 2008) or very fast presentation rates (e.g., Yonelinas, Hockley, & Murdock, 1992) may result in low recall rates.
Typically, participants have reduced recall of the forgotten material compared to the material to remember (Geiselman and Bagheri 1985; Sahakyan and Delaney 2005;  Sahakyan et al. 2008 ).

As Sahakyan et al. (2008a) pointed out, older adults may also not use forgetting strategies spontaneously to the same extend as younger adults do; a mental context change is then hardly initiated at all.

Sahakyan et al. (2008a) suggest that whether older adults will show directed forgetting costs in list method studies depends on whether they engage in active forgetting strategies; such strategies are a prerequisite to initiate a mental context change.
